newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Rebels seize 19 MiGs at Albania airbase.
newsitem.headline: Rebels seize 19 MiGs at Albania airbase.

text.p: The capture of a key airbase by armed insurgents in southern Albania has left about one fifth of the country's warplanes in rebel hands.

The airbase at Kucove, overrun on Monday by angry rebels demanding the resignation of President Sali Berisha following the collapse of pyramid investment schemes, is also the site of the country's air force maintenance and repair unit.
In the nearby town, insurgents burned out the police station, witnesses said.

At the airbase, angry pilots in front of a line of 19 ageing MiG warplanes spoke of how they had lost their savings in pyramid investment schemes whose collapse has plunged Albania into crisis, and declared they could not obey orders to defy the insurgents.
The authoritative London based International Institute for Strategic Studies says the Albanian air force has 98 combat aircraft.

The air force has not played a major role so far in Albania's crisis but the capture of a large number of warplanes, alongside the tanks and guns already seized by the rebels, is an embarrassment for the government.

An Albanian MiG 15 flew to Italy last week and its two pilots told Italian reporters they had defected rather than carry out orders to shoot at civilians. Albania denied their version, saying they had been on a reconnaissance mission.

The air force officers at Kucove said base commanders had ordered that machine-guns be fired to frighten crowds who seized the base about 100 km (60 miles) south of the capital, Tirana, as the country's armed uprising spread on Monday.
"We were given an order to fire to frighten the crowds but I could not find it in my heart to do it," said one pilot who declined to give his name.

Twenty-four hours after they overran the airfield, young men roamed the area firing looted Kalashnikov assault rifles into the air in what has become the trademark gesture of the rebels who have taken over much of southern Albania.
They too had lost money in the pyramid investment schemes and they blamed Berisha for their loss.
"Everybody here had accounts in the banks and we lost all our money," said one young man brandishing two assault rifles.
"We are not rebels, we are the people. We like democracy and we want our money back."

As he spoke other local people were taking direct action to redress at least some of their loss, loading up bundles of firewood onto carts and walking off with furniture and other goods looted from the barracks.
Shepherds sporting military tin helmets were grazing their sheep and goats on the grass of the airbase football pitch laid out between gun emplacements.
Communist leader Enver Hoxha, whose isolationist rule ended in 1985, built more than 700,000 concrete pill boxes to protect Albania from foreign invaders.
Those surrounding the Kucove airbase had however proved ineffective against Albania's own angry citizens.

In the nearby town, insurgents burned out the police station and set up their own checkpoint. Fierce-looking men with pink and blue ribbons tied round their gun barrels stopped cars and questioned drivers.
Not far from the town, a group of up to 50 Albanian soldiers who said they had defected from near the southern town of Vlore were looking for a truck to take them home.
"I don't want to fight my father, my friends, my brothers," said one soldier, who declined to be identified. "I only like to fight against Albania's enemies, not against my people."
